title: Recovering approval winners from ranked ballots: best–worst voting and the approval-compatibility questions of Terzopoulou, Lang and Zwicker
oneLine: One point for first, minus one for last: an exact answer to an open question on approval-compatible voting rules
abstract: Suppose voters who cast approval ballots each submit a ranking that puts their approved candidates above the others. Can a positional scoring rule applied to such sincere rankings reproduce the approval result? Terzopoulou, Lang and Zwicker (Social Choice and Welfare, 2025) showed that Borda voting can make all approval co-winners win together once every ballot is replicated, that no other scoring rule can with three candidates, and asked whether Borda is unique for more candidates. This candidate shows that it is not. Best–worst voting, one point for first place and minus one for last, recovers the approval winner set exactly for every number m ≥ 3 of candidates with at most m − 1 copies of each ballot, and one voter can force that many. A polynomial-time test decides the property for any rational scoring vector; with it the rules that have the property are classified for four and five candidates and, among rational rules, for six. For the weaker requirement that each approval winner can be elected separately, the scalar inequalities those authors proved necessary are shown sufficient for every real scoring vector when a ballot may be split between rankings, and for every rational vector under replication; with whole copies and irrational scores an eight-candidate, five-ballot example shows the conjecture can fail. Limits: results concern the existence of sincere rankings in the worst case, not voter behaviour; irrational six-candidate rules and general m remain open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: A 14-page paper with a context-first introduction, written proofs of every result, limits, open problems and an AI-use statement. Three Python programs in exact integer or rational arithmetic accompany it: verify_endpoints.py checks the rational certificates (3,600 inequalities for four candidates, 30,752 for five and 254,016 for each of three six-candidate corner rules), the two six-candidate witness elections and the eight-candidate counterexample; verify_rational_fpac.py checks the 18 + 18 signed vertex cases of the one-winner criterion; check_best_worst.py checks all one- and two-voter elections with three to five candidates. A clean replay in Python's optimised mode reproduced the recorded outputs; changing one certificate entry makes verify_endpoints.py fail; Linux CI reruns all three.

keyResults: Theorem 5 (proof): best–worst voting (1, 0, …, 0, −1) makes exactly the approval winners win after at most m − 1 copies of each ballot, for every m ≥ 3; one voter can force m − 1. Since (2, 1, 1, 0) is best–worst voting for four candidates, Borda is not the only such rule for any m ≥ 4.
Theorem 8 and Lemma 9 (proof): a polynomial-time test of the property for rational scoring vectors; every rule with the property is reflection symmetric.

Theorems 10 and 12 (proof with exact certificates): the rules with the property for four and five candidates, and the rational rules for six, whose gaps (g2, g3) form the quadrilateral with corners (0, 0), (0, 3), (5/4, 11/2) and (4, 0). The four-candidate necessity is due to Terzopoulou, Lang and Zwicker.

Theorem 13 and Corollary 14 (proof): the scalar inequalities of Terzopoulou, Lang and Zwicker suffice for each approval winner to be elected separately, for real scores when ballots may be split and for rational scores under replication.

Theorem 15 and Corollary 16 (proof): in an eight-candidate, five-ballot election, a finite replication elects the designated candidate exactly when a parameter of the rule is rational, and the copies needed can be arbitrarily large.

Credit and limits: Terzopoulou, Lang and Zwicker (question, Borda result, four-candidate necessary condition, scalar inequalities and conjecture), Edmonds (greedy method), Baumeister–Rothe and Kenig (possible winner problem). Existence of sincere rankings only; worst-case; irrational six-candidate rules and general m open.
